Dual Copper/Photoredox Catalysis: Photoreductive 1,4-
Dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-Enynes with Dibenzothiophenium
Salts and Trimethylsilyl Cyanide

ABSTRACT: A photoredox and copper dual-catalyzed 1,4-
arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes has been established using aryldibenzo-
thiophenium salts (Ar-DBT
+
) as aryl radical precursors, affording a
wide array of tetra-substituted allenes with high chemo- and
regioselectivity. This strategy exhibits a broad substrate scope with
remarkable functional group tolerance, all under mild conditions.
Notably, this process generates tetra-substituted allenes in a one-
step reaction through the use of various electron-rich and electron-
deficient aryldibenzothiophenium salts.
A
llenes serve as valuable structural motifs in natural
products and biologically active molecules, attracting
considerable attention for the development of efficient
synthetic methods to construct diverse functionalized allene
structures (Figure 1).
1
In particular, 1,4-functionalizations of
1,3-enynes provide a concise and efficient synthetic strategy,
enabling the simultaneous introduction of two functional
groups with high regio-, chemo-, and stereocontrol.
2,3
While
most methods focus on allenyl anions or allenyl cations via
transition-metal catalysis,
4
radical-based 1,4-difunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes has emerged as a novel and increasingly popular
approach for the synthesizing tetra-substituted allenes.
3
For
instance, the groups of Bao
3c
and Liu
3d
independently
described a Cu-catalyzed enantioselective process for synthe-
sizing chiral allenes via the radical 1,4-dicarbylation of 1,3-
enynes (Scheme 1a). Subsequently, Chen and co-workers
reported an organocatalytic 1,4-alkylacylation of 1,3-enynes in
the presence of an aldehyde, CF
3
radical precursor, and an N-
heterocyclic carbene catalyst, enabling the synthesis of various
tetrasubstituted allenes under mild conditions (Scheme 1b).
3e
Recently, Yao’s group developed a nickel-catalyzed method for
synthesizing 1,4-difunctionalized allenes utilizing a novel chiral
bulk bis-oxazoline ligand in a radical tandem process (Scheme
1c).
3f
Notably, numerous strategies combining photo- and
electrochemistry with transition metal catalysis or organo-
catalysis have emerged for the radical 1,4-difunctionalization of
1,3-enynes, offering efficient synthesis of structurally diverse
allene products (Scheme 1d).
3i−p
While numerous studies have
been conducted on the 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes
via radical pathways, several persistent challenges remain
unresolved. These include: (i) the short-lived nature of allenyl
radical intermediates, (ii) difficulties with regiocontrol, and
(iii) competition between 1,2- and 1,4-addition pathways in
the transformation of 1,3-enynes. To date, all reported
methods have focused exclusively on alkyl radical-involved
1,4-difunctionalization for constructing tetrasubstituted allenes,
with transformations employing aryl radicals remaining

Therefore, expanding the synthetic
utility of these reactions requires exploring different radical
precursors, particularly aryl radicals.
Arylsulfonium salts have been investigated as aryl radical
precursors in photocatalyzed reactions. Pioneering works by
the groups of Ritter,
6
Procter,
7
Wang,
8
Rueping
9
and others
10
have made significant contributions in this area. Among these,
aryldibenzothiophenium salts have garnered attention as
versatile coupling partners derived from simple arenes, capable
of generating aryl radical intermediates through photoredox-
catalyzed transformations for arene functionalization. Very
recently, a metal-free photoredox-catalyzed three-component
synthesis of aryl sulfonamides was developed employing
dibenzothiophenium (DBT) as the radical precursor.
11
Inspired by these elegant studies, we envisioned utilizing an
Ar-DBT
+
ion derived from an arene to generate an aryl radical
under photoredox conditions. The aryl radical would then be
trapped by 1,3-enynes, leading to the formation of highly
reactive allenyl radicals, which could be captured by a suitable
copper catalyst complex. Reductive elimination of the complex
would yield multisubstituted allenes (Scheme 1B). During this
process, a single-electron transfer (SET) from the excited-state
photocatalyst to Ar-DBT
+
would generate dibenzothiophene
and the aryl radical species. To the best of our knowledge, this
is the first report documenting the use of dibenzothiophenium
salts as aryl group precursors to enable the 1,4-difunctionaliza-
tion of 1,3-enynes, and our strategy provides a general avenue
to polysubstituted allenes. This reaction represents a new
strategy for the synthesis of polysubstituted allenes scaffolds
using simple and readily available starting materials (Scheme
1B).
Herein, we initiated optimization studies by investigating the
three-component reaction of 1,3-enyne 1a with 4-MeO-aryl
DBT salt 2a and trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) 3a by visible
light photoredox catalysis (Table 1). Detailed screening
experiments are provided in the Supporting Information.
Intriguingly, using fac-Ir(ppy)
3
(1 mol %) as the photocatalyst
under 36 W blue light-emitting diodes (LEDs), along with
[Cu(MeCN)
4
]PF
6
(10 mol %), ligand L4 (14 mol %) and
DMSO as the solvent, the desired product 4a was obtained in
50% yield after 48 h under an argon atmosphere (entry 1).
Systematic screening of the reaction conditions revealed that
the combination of blue light, [Cu(MeCN)
4
]PF
6
, and the
photocatalyst were critical for the reaction’s success, as
omitting any of these components led to no detectable 4a as
the product (entries 2−4). It is noteworthy that when the
reaction was carried out in 60 °C in the absence of visible light,
no desired product was obtained (entry 5). The product was
still obtained without 4,4′-dibromo-2,2′-bipyridine (L4) or 4 Å
MS, but in lower yields (entries 6−7). Varying the molar ratio
of 1a, 2a and 3a to 1:1.5:1.5, resulted in a decrease in yield of
product 4a to 38% (entry 8). Increasing the photocatalyst to 3
mol % decreased the yield of the product 4a in 45% yield
(entry 9), while decreasing the amount of [Cu(MeCN)
4
]PF
6
or increasing ligand loading did not enhance reaction yields
(entries 10−11). Various copper catalysts were screened
(entries 12−15), including [Cu(MeCN)
4
]BF
4

2

and CuOTf, but these gave unfavorable results. Replacing
DMSO with other solvents, such as DMF, toluene or MeCN,
resulted in negligible product formation (entries 16−18).

Next, we explored the scope of 1,3-enyne 1 and aryl-DBT
salts 2 using 3a as the reaction partner. As shown in Scheme 3,
a range of substituted anisole-derived aryl-DBT salts were
tested to assess the compatibility of various functional groups.
Reactions of 1,2-dimethoxybenzene nd 1,4-benzodioxane
derivatives proceeded smoothly to provide 5a and 5b in 29%
and 38% yields, respectively. Aryl-DBT salts bearing Cl, Br,
and COOMe functionalities in the ortho-position to OMe were
also compatible, delivering the desired allenes 5c−5e in 27−
37% yields, offering potential for further derivatization of the

To demonstrate the synthetic utility of this protocol, we
performed further transformations of 4a (Scheme 4). For
example, reduction with DIBAL-H selectively converts the
cyano group into an aldehyde, yielding product 6 in 68% yield.
Subsequent reduction of the product 6 afforded the
corresponding alcohol 7 in 64% yield. Treatment of product
7 with NBS led to the cyclized brominated product 8 in 67%
yield.
3k
When we conducted the nitrile hydrolysis under basic
conditions,
12
the desired allenic amide product could not be
obtained. Instead, a Michael addition side reaction occurred at
the central carbon of the allene system, resulting in the
formation of a tetra-substituted alkene 9.
To further gain mechanistic insights into the reaction, a few
control experiments were conducted. When the radical
scavenger TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinooxy) was
added, the 1,4-arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes was almost fully
inhibited (Scheme 5a). In addition, the radical-trapped
product 11 was isolated in 80% yield, when 4.0 equiv of 1,1-
diphenylethylene was added to the reaction. These results
indicated that an aryl radical is involved in this process

The light on/off experiments showed that continuous

In summary, we have developed a copper/photoredox dual
catalyzed 1,4-arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes using aryldibenzo-
thiophenium salts (Ar-DBT
+
) as aryl radical precursors, for the
synthesis of tetra-substituted allenes. The reaction operates
under mild conditions, offering excellent chemo- and
regioselectivity while maintaining broad functional group
compatibility. The scope of the reaction is extensive, and we
believe this methodology provides a novel and versatile
synthetic approach to the multifunctionalization of 1,3-enynes
and related compounds, with significant conceptual implica-
tions for synthetic chemistry.

ABSTRACT: A photoredox and copper dual-catalyzed 1,4-
arylcyanation of 1,3-enynes has been established using aryldibenzo-
thiophenium salts (Ar-DBT<sup>+</sup>) as aryl radical precursors, afording a
wide array of tetra-substituted allenes with high chemo- and
regioselectivity. This strategy exhibits a broad substrate scope with
remarkable functional group tolerance, all under mild conditions.
Notably, this process generates tetra-substituted allenes in a one-
step reaction through the use of various electron-rich and electron-
deficient aryldibenzothiophenium salts.

Arylsulfonium salts have been investigated as aryl radical
precursors in photocatalyzed reactions. Pioneering works by
the groups of Ritter,<sup>6</sup> Procter,<sup>7</sup> Wang,<sup>8</sup> Rueping<sup>9</sup> and others<sup>10</sup>

versatile coupling partners derived from simple arenes, capable
of generating aryl radical intermediates through photoredox-
catalyzed transformations for arene functionalization. Very
recently, a metal-free photoredox-catalyzed three-component
synthesis of aryl sulfonamides was developed employing
dibenzothiophenium (DBT) as the radical precursor.

reactive allenyl radicals, which could be captured by a suitable
copper catalyst complex. Reductive elimination of the complex
